title: 1 Kings 11:14–25
context: God raises up adversaries against Solomon: Hadad the Edomite, who had fled to Egypt as a child after David’s campaign in Edom and later returned, and Rezon, who seized power in Damascus. The text attributes their rise to God, while recounting their own choices and grievances. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s providence and discipline, holding God’s rule and human responsibility together without explaining how they relate.

verses.text: The LORD raised up an adversary to Solomon: Hadad the Edomite. He was one of the king’s offspring in Edom.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD raises up Hadad the Edomite, of the royal family, as an adversary to Solomon. Judgment begins through enemies.

Arminian readers see God directing Hadad’s existing hostility toward Solomon as discipline.
verses.reformedNotes:
The text says plainly that the LORD raised him up. God governs even Solomon’s opponents.

Reformed readers see God’s providence ordering events to discipline his servant. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s providence and judgment, while holding Hadad responsible for his own choices.

verses.text: For when David was in Edom, and Joab the captain of the army had gone up to bury the slain, and had struck every male in Edom
verses.arminianNotes:
When David was in Edom, Joab went to bury the slain and struck down every male. The narrative recalls past warfare.

Arminian readers see past violence shaping present enmity. The past is not forgotten by those who suffered it.
verses.reformedNotes:
The background recalls David’s campaign in Edom (compare 2 Samuel 8:13–14). Hadad’s grievance has roots.

Reformed readers see history’s long consequences. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without speculating beyond what the text says about the campaign.

verses.text: (for Joab and all Israel remained there six months, until he had cut off every male in Edom),
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab and Israel remained six months until every male in Edom was cut off. The parenthesis explains the severity.

Arminian readers note the narrator reports the campaign without commentary. The severity of that campaign helps explain lasting enmity.
verses.reformedNotes:
The parenthetical detail explains why Hadad fled. The narrative does not evaluate the campaign here.

Reformed readers likewise read it plainly. Both traditions treat this as shared ground, recognizing that the account describes events rather than commending them, and that Hadad’s hostility grows from them.

verses.text: Hadad fled, he and certain Edomites of his father’s servants with him, to go into Egypt, when Hadad was still a little child.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hadad, still a little child, fled to Egypt with some of his father’s servants. He survived.

Arminian readers see a young survivor whose life is preserved for a later role.
verses.reformedNotes:
The child’s escape preserves a royal line of Edom. The narrator traces how Hadad came to oppose Solomon.

Reformed readers see providence preserving even an enemy for God’s purposes. Both traditions read this as shared ground, without making it more than the text says.

verses.text: They arose out of Midian and came to Paran; and they took men with them out of Paran, and they came to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt, who gave him a house, and appointed him food, and gave him land.
verses.arminianNotes:
They traveled from Midian to Paran and on to Egypt, where Pharaoh gave Hadad a house, food, and land. Egypt welcomed him.

Arminian readers see political circumstances favoring Hadad’s survival.
verses.reformedNotes:
Pharaoh’s generosity provides Hadad with security. The route is described briefly; precise locations are not certain.

Reformed readers see God working through foreign rulers. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hold geographic details lightly.

verses.text: Hadad found great favor in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him as wife the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hadad found such favor with Pharaoh that he married the sister of Queen Tahpenes. He became part of Egypt’s royal household.

Arminian readers see alliances that strengthen Hadad’s position. Hadad’s standing in Egypt grows steadily.
verses.reformedNotes:
Marriage into Pharaoh’s family gave Hadad standing. The detail parallels Solomon’s own marriage to Pharaoh’s daughter (11:1).

Reformed readers see the irony of shared alliances. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting the narrative’s interest in how political ties shape history.

verses.text: The sister of Tahpenes bore him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh’s house; and Genubath was in Pharaoh’s house among the sons of Pharaoh.
verses.arminianNotes:
Tahpenes’ sister bore Genubath, raised among Pharaoh’s sons. Hadad’s family is established in Egypt.

Arminian readers see Hadad settled and secure before returning. His roots in Egypt run deep, yet his heart remains with Edom.
verses.reformedNotes:
The son’s upbringing in Pharaoh’s house underscores Hadad’s prominence. The narrator includes it as part of the background.

Reformed readers see the steady preparation of an adversary. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground and do not draw further conclusions from the family detail.

verses.text: When Hadad heard in Egypt that David slept with his fathers, and that Joab the captain of the army was dead, Hadad said to Pharaoh, “Let me depart, that I may go to my own country.”
verses.arminianNotes:
When Hadad heard that David and Joab were dead, he asked Pharaoh to let him return home. He waits for his moment.

Arminian readers see Hadad choosing to return when circumstances change.
verses.reformedNotes:
The deaths of David and Joab open the door. Hadad seeks to go back.

Reformed readers see providence aligning events for Solomon’s discipline. Both traditions read this as shared ground, holding Hadad’s choices and God’s purpose together without explaining how.

verses.text: Then Pharaoh said to him, “But what have you lacked with me, that behold, you seek to go to your own country?” He answered, “Nothing, however only let me depart.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Pharaoh asks what he lacks; Hadad says nothing, but still asks to leave. His desire is to return.

Arminian readers see a free decision driven by loyalty to his homeland.
verses.reformedNotes:
Hadad has every comfort but wants to go home. His motive is not fully explained.

Reformed readers see God’s purpose working through ordinary human longing. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without inventing motives the text does not state.

verses.text: God raised up an adversary to him, Rezon the son of Eliada, who had fled from his lord, Hadadezer king of Zobah.
verses.arminianNotes:
God raises up another adversary, Rezon son of Eliada, who had fled from Hadadezer king of Zobah. Opposition increases.

Arminian readers see God directing existing hostilities as part of Solomon’s discipline.
verses.reformedNotes:
The text again says God raised him up. Hadadezer was defeated by David (2 Samuel 8:3).

Reformed readers see God’s providence over Solomon’s enemies. Both traditions read this as shared ground, affirming God’s rule and Rezon’s responsibility together.

verses.text: He gathered men to himself, and became captain over a troop, when David killed them of Zobah. They went to Damascus and lived there, and reigned in Damascus.
verses.arminianNotes:
Rezon gathers men, becomes a band leader after David’s defeat of Zobah, and reigns in Damascus. He builds power.

Arminian readers see an opportunist rising through circumstances. Ambition and opportunity combine in his rise to power.
verses.reformedNotes:
Rezon’s rise establishes a rival power to the north. Damascus will become significant in later Kings.

Reformed readers see God’s purposes extending into future history. Both traditions read this as shared ground, without asserting chronological details the text does not specify.

verses.text: He was an adversary to Israel all the days of Solomon, in addition to the mischief of Hadad. He abhorred Israel, and reigned over Syria.
verses.arminianNotes:
Rezon is Israel’s adversary throughout Solomon’s reign, adding to Hadad’s trouble; he hated Israel and ruled Syria. Solomon’s peace is undermined.

Arminian readers see the consequences of Solomon’s apostasy unfolding.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator links both adversaries to God’s judgment. Solomon’s reign is no longer untroubled.

Reformed readers see discipline that warns rather than destroys. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s providence and judgment on idolatry.
